newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW -- UK second quarter GDP data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- UK second quarter GDP data.

text.p: Following is a selection of economists' reactions to data showing UK GDP grew a preliminary 0.9 percent in the second quarter from the previous quarter and was up 3.4 percent year-on-year (this was in line with the Reuters consensus forecast):
PETER LUXTON, MMS INTERNATIONAL "It is well above trend
growth and it does keep the alert on for higher interest rates."
"The question is timing -- when not if. Will they go in August or wait a bit to see the details after a couple of months' data and go in September?"

"The figures are in line with market expectations. They still confirm that the economy is growing more strongly certainly than the Bank of England would want. What will concern them is the buoyancy of the service sector, which very much reinforced what we saw in this week's retail sales figures. It does increase the pressure for a rate hike. These figures by themselves won't prompt a rate hike but certainly I think there is a strong possibility they could move as early as August."

"Q2 GDP was a touch softer than expected at 0.9 percent on the quarter but this reflected weakness in the energy sector. More significantly, non-energy was up a firm 3.6 percent on the year and services sector growth surged to some 4.5 percent. This latter pickup will worry the Bank of England since this is where the real threat to inflation lies. Data should be seen as strong enough to keep alive speculation about a rate hike next month and to this end, should be seen as supportive of the pound while keeping the curve -- particularly at the short end -- under pressure. Our bet is still just about no hike until the September MPC meeting but today's data do nothing to reduce the risk of a move next month. Gap between services and manufacturing again underscores the policy dilemma facing the Bank and we think ought to be enough for the MPC to bide their time for now."

"Fairly well in line with expectations but a touch softer than we had predicted. The service sector is still the key area -- up 1.3 per cent q/q is still pretty strong -- and it looks like industrial production has been weak, with sterling possibly doing some damage now on the manufacturing side. Over the quarter, manufacturing is going to be flat. Still good strong economic growth but increasingly it is being driven by services rather than manufacturing. Again it highlights the dilemma for policy makers -- sterling is very strong so if you put rates up to try to slow down some of this domestic demand driven growth, you risk further hurting the output and manufacturing side."
